MOONSLIP

My launch slipped N days. Is my landing site still survivable, and what is the best alternate site or date?

Click the lander to land ↗
01 / Our purpose

A few days of delay can turn a good landing site into a dark one.

Near the lunar south pole the Sun grazes the horizon and Earth dips in and out of view. Slip-Recovery Planner tells a mission planner, in about ten seconds, whether a site still works after a launch delay, how much margin is left, and where or when to go instead.

02 / How it works

Three inputs. One verdict you can defend.

Step 1

Pick a site and a date

Eleven sites from Apollo 11 to the Shackleton ridge, any landing date from 1 December 2026 to 30 November 2027.

Step 2

Enter the launch slip

Type or drag the number of days. The landing slips by the same amount and every verdict is recomputed at once.

Step 3

Read the verdict

Green, Yellow or Red from a written, adjustable formula, with the days of margin left, the next good window and the best alternate site.

04 / Data and method

Computed in advance, checked in the open.

Every number in the planner comes from one data file written by a Google Colab notebook. The page does no astronomy itself; it only reads the file and applies the verdict formula you can see and change.

Sun, Earth and Moon positionsNASA JPL DE421 ephemeris, read with Skyfield 1.55Sun and Earth direction every hour for 12 months
Moon orientationNAIF lunar kernels, frame MOON_ME_DE421Fixes each site to the rotating Moon, so libration is included
Independent checkNASA JPL Horizons18 values compared at nine site and time pairs
TerrainNASA LRO LOLA LDEM_75S_120M, 120 m per pixel360-direction skyline for the five sites within 10° of the south pole
Lander coordinatesNSSDC tables of spacecraft on the MoonLatitude and longitude of the eight lander sites
Ridge points A, C, M1Bussey et al. 2010Each moved up to 1.07 km to the highest nearby ground on the LOLA map

Verdict formula
How the verdict is decided

Red if, during the mission, any of these is true: the Sun is below the minimum elevation at landing; the longest continuous dark stretch is longer than the maximum eclipse; or (comms required) Earth is below the horizon at landing or hidden for longer than the maximum comms gap. Yellow if the mission passes but would fail when extended by the buffer. Green otherwise. Landing is taken at 00:00 UTC on each date. Durations are accurate to one data step. Lander type fills in starting values: a day lander runs on solar power and tolerates only a short shadow (6 h); a night survivor has heaters or stored power for a full lunar night (up to 380 h).

Full data

Validation, terrain checks and data format

Notebook output against JPL Horizons (18 values)

Terrain check: our height map against published values

SiteCheckOursReferenceDifference
IM-1 OdysseusGround elevation2,585 m2,579 m (NASA LRO image release)+6 m
IM-1 OdysseusGround elevation2,585 m2,590 m (LROC QuickMap TerrainHeight, 3 m per pixel)-5 m
IM-2 AthenaGround elevation5,324 m5,321 m (LROC QuickMap TerrainHeight, 4 m per pixel)+3 m

Ours: NASA LOLA LDEM_75S_120M at 120 m per pixel. Ground elevation is height above the 1737.4 km reference sphere. Our 120 m pixels average the ground over a wider patch than QuickMap's 3 to 4 m pixels, so a few metres of difference on a slope is expected. QuickMap values were read by the team on 14 Nov 2026 at points placed at 80.13°S 1.44°E and 84.79°S 29.20°E. QuickMap also reports local slope: 12.2° at IM-1 (NASA states 12°) and 2.4° at IM-2; the verdict does not use slope. Sites north of 75°S are outside our height map and show no elevation.

Data contract v1.0 (what the Colab notebook writes and this app reads)

{ "meta": { "contract":"1.0", "source":"text", "frame":"MOON_ME",
    "start_utc":"2026-12-01T00:00:00Z", "step_hours":1, "n_steps":8760,
    "terrain":false, "validated":false },
  "sites": [ { "id":"a11", "name":"Apollo 11", "lat":0.67, "lon":23.47,
      "verified":false, "source":"text", "elev_km":2.585,
      "sun_el":[..], "sun_az":[..], "earth_el":[..], "earth_az":[..],
      "horizon":[..360 values, optional..] } ] }
All angles in degrees. lat north-positive, lon east-positive (-180..180).
az clockwise from north; el above a smooth-sphere horizon.
Each of the four arrays has n_steps numbers; step i is start_utc + i*step_hours.
start_utc must be at 00:00 UTC. horizon[k] = terrain elevation angle at azimuth k deg.
elev_km (optional, added 14 Nov) = ground height above the 1737.4 km sphere.

Use the Load data.json button, or put data.json next to index.html when deploying. Until real data is loaded, every number on this page comes from a toy model and is not real.
